flawed_step: Step 1 (existence) is fine: Gale–Shapley always gives a stable matching. Step 2 (uniqueness) fails. To show uniqueness you would have to prove that the men-proposing and women-proposing Gale–Shapley matchings are always the same. Strict, complete preferences do not force this.
counterexample: n=2. Men: m1 ranks w1 > w2, and m2 ranks w2 > w1. Women: w1 ranks m2 > m1, and w2 ranks m1 > m2. Matching A = {(m1,w1),(m2,w2)} is stable because each man has his first choice, so no man would join a blocking pair. Matching B = {(m1,w2),(m2,w1)} is stable because each woman has her first choice. That gives two different stable matchings.
assessment_summary: Following the proof order: a stable matching always exists (Gale–Shapley), but the uniqueness step cannot be justified. The 2x2 instance with opposite preferences has two stable matchings: the men-optimal one and the women-optimal one. So the statement is false in general.
